case_notes.content:
Initial Meeting and Background  
• Isaiah introduced himself to Kevin; referred by Tori, visited the previous day.  
• Recently released from jail after two years; has a pending armed robbery charge (attorney expects it to be dropped).  
• Previous arrests: simple possession (2011, a few hours in jail), credit card theft (2022, one day in jail).  
• Struggled with addiction (opioids, cocaine, Xanax, fentanyl) and PTSD (brother died in his arms from gun violence ~10 years ago).  
• Used substances to cope with PTSD; started with Xanax, escalated to opioids and alcohol, then fentanyl.  
• Continued substance use during first year in jail; found it easier to access drugs inside than outside.  
• Entered DAODAS program in jail; sober date June 29, 2025 (entered program ~15-16 months ago).  
• Stayed in DAODAS for a year (program is four months) due to not feeling ready for release.  
• Earned 40 certificates on Edovo, 2 from DAODAS, Seeking Safety, Favor Low Country, and 6 character letters.  
• Released on PR bond; judge considered his rehabilitation efforts.  
• Knows Chris Cherry (formerly Favor, now Recovery Unplugged); Chris wrote him a letter of support.  

Current Living Situation and Needs  
• Lives at an Oxford House near the center (10 minutes away).  
• Main barriers: lack of income, need to pay Oxford House, desire to buy a car, lacks clothes and possessions (lost during arrest).  
• Starting from scratch after release; apartment and car were lost.  

Details of Pending Charge  
• Clarified the charge: not an armed robbery, but a dispute with a drug dealer over payment (Cash App vs. cash).  
• Physical altercation occurred; dealer accused Isaiah of robbery to neighbors and police.  
• Police detained and arrested Isaiah; searched his house but found no weapon or stolen items.  
• Dealer claimed Isaiah lured him via Facebook and robbed him; later, body cam footage showed the dealer had his wallet.  
• Bond set at $60,000; dealer has been unresponsive to solicitor’s attempts to contact.  
• Public defender is Helen Dovell; Isaiah is satisfied with her efforts.  

Program Offerings and Structure  
• Kevin explained Turn 90’s services:  
  ◦ Resource coordination: statewide, free, helps justice-involved individuals find community resources.  
  ◦ Reentry navigation: deeper, ongoing support for legal, housing, employment, medical, and mental health needs.  
  ◦ First Shift: paid program (Monday–Friday, 9:00–3:00), includes:  
    ▪ Q1 & Q3: cognitive behavioral treatment (CBT) skills, similar to DAODAS.  
    ▪ Q2: trades curriculum (hands-on and computer-based), e.g., electrical, HVAC, plumbing, forklift certification, OSHA 10.  
    ▪ Employer relationships for job placement.  
    ▪ Educational stipend up to $450/week, based on points for attendance, phone use, and homework.  
    ▪ Currently a waitlist (~2 weeks); can start with reentry navigation in the meantime.  
• Isaiah can work on resume and job search while waiting.  

Isaiah’s Skills, Experience, and Goals  
• Has a resume; applied to Carrabba’s (previous employer, 6 years at Mount Pleasant location).  
• Completed Edovo courses in jail, focusing on challenging certificates related to recovery and reentry.  
• Completed Edwin’s Restaurant curriculum (culinary skills) via Edovo; aspires to be a chef.  
• Interested in Edwin’s in Cleveland (paid training, housing support), but cannot attend until case is resolved.  
• Open to learning new skills in the meantime; does not want to be a “one-trick pony.”  
• Edwin’s hires people with criminal backgrounds, but pending charge is a barrier.  
• Uploaded resume to Indeed as soon as he got a phone.  

Housing Choice and Recovery  
• Chose Oxford House over living with mother to avoid old environment and negative influences in Mount Pleasant.  
• Lived near mother previously, but wants to maintain recovery by staying in a new environment.  

Next Steps and Communication  
• Provided phone number (854-291-4520) for follow-up.  
• Kevin will text Isaiah from a program number (shared with program manager) for ongoing communication.  
• Possible orientation next Friday at 3:30pm; could start First Shift the following Monday if a spot opens.  
• If Isaiah finds a better job, he can remain in reentry navigation for continued support.  
• Reentry navigation includes accountability (e.g., following up on tasks like DMV visits for license issues).  
• Can continue to access support remotely if employed elsewhere.  

Program and Court Requirements  
• Turn 90 classes may count toward required AA meetings for Oxford House/court; classes focus on control, decision-making, and recovery skills.  
• Courts and Oxford House often accept Turn 90 participation as fulfilling AA requirements.  
• Kevin can advocate to courts/public defender regarding Isaiah’s participation.  

Medical and Mental Health Support  
• Isaiah was prescribed Suboxone before release; received a one-week bridge script, but missed follow-up at Charleston Center due to interview.  
• Appointment rescheduled for next Wednesday; concerned about running out of Suboxone and withdrawal.  
• Spoke to Jessica Rivon (Charleston Center); awaiting further instructions for another bridge script.  
• Kevin suggested free clinic (with psychiatrists, non-addictive meds) and Well Vista (SC program for medical care and transportation).  
• Isaiah previously prescribed Prazosin for nightmares (PTSD); wants to resume medication.  
• Can discuss PTSD and medication needs with Turn 90’s doctors or via Well Vista.  
• Clinic prefers non-addictive medications; Kevin shared his own experience with Wellbutrin.  

Employment and Scheduling  
• Isaiah has a potential night shift job; wants to coordinate with Turn 90’s 9:00–3:00 schedule.  
• Kevin encourages Isaiah to do what’s best for him; Turn 90 can still provide support regardless of employment status.  
• Can connect Isaiah with Chris Cherry (Recovery Unplugged) and Mike Jackson (Favor Low Country) for additional support and referrals.  
• Isaiah has already reached out to Mike Jackson upon release.  

Ongoing Support and Follow-Up  
• Kevin will keep Isaiah updated on waitlist status and connect him with Chris Cherry.  
• Will maintain communication to address needs as they arise and help assemble resources.  
• Encouraged Isaiah to take water and closed the meeting.

He lost a cousin to a fatal fentanyl overdose involving contaminated cocaine. Since being released from custody, he has remained completely sober, going "cold turkey" and distancing himself from peers who still engage in drug use.


* **Family Background & Parental Drivers:** The participant grew up in foster care starting around age 6 after his mother left. He recently reconnected with a 4-year-old son whom he initially did not know existed until a DNA test confirmed paternity following his release from prison. His primary motivation to stay clean and succeed is to be a stable father, break the cycle of abandonment he experienced, and provide a room and home for his son.


* **Legal Status & Defense:** The participant faces pending charges (including trafficking, cocaine, marijuana, and ecstasy). He is represented by Public Defender **Patrick Goodwin**. His attorney and the solicitor are supportive of him completing a drug court/CBT program as an alternative to mandatory sentence requirements.


* **Certifications & Progress:** While previously in county custody, the participant earned several credentials, including a **WorkKeys Level 3**, **OSHA Certification**, and a **Psychosocial Certificate**, alongside parenting classes.

    ▪ Points for attendance, participation, and homework completion.  
    ▪ Includes certifications, thinking and emotion regulation skills.  
    ▪ Employers willing to overlook criminal backgrounds based on program performance.  
    ▪ Currently has a waitlist (3–6 weeks).  
    ▪ Participants may move between programs as needed (e.g., due to accidents or setbacks).  

Client Background and Legal Status  
• Recently released from Alamance jail after about a year.  
• Has pending charges:  
  ◦ Trafficking fentanyl (test showed it was not fentanyl; lawyer seeking to get charge dropped).  
  ◦ Possession with intent (PWID) marijuana, possession of ecstasy.

• Lawyer and solicitor recommend program participation to support court outcomes.  
• Drug court is a likely option; client unfamiliar but open to it.

• Client desires independent housing but is content for now.

  ◦ Discovered son’s existence while in prison; confirmed paternity after release.  
  ◦ Had custody for three months post-release before returning son to mother due to job loss and instability.  
  ◦ Relationship with son’s mother is good; she desires a two-parent home.  
• Limited family support:  
  ◦ Mother in rehab, does not know father, grandparents deceased.  
  ◦ Older brother incarcerated and struggling with addiction.  
  ◦ Family history of addiction and foster care involvement.  
• Client values family and seeks to provide support, despite limited reciprocal support.  

Substance Use and Recovery

  ◦ Usage was social/recreational, not perceived as problematic by client.  
  ◦ Drug use increased after losing job and custody of son.  
• No substance use since release; committed to complete sobriety, motivated by son and recent experiences.  
• No current mental health or medical concerns.  
  ◦ Childhood ADHD diagnosis and psychiatric medication until age 14; no treatment since.

• Resume development and job search support to be provided by Daisy.  
  ◦ Staff Zone and Alternative Staffing suggested as immediate options.  
  ◦ Center has relationships with felon-friendly employers and some housing providers.  

Transportation and Housing

• No driver’s license; never had one, has history of DUS (driving under suspension).  
  ◦ Obtaining a license is a priority for independence and employment.

  ◦ Center can assist with independent housing search when ready; felon-friendly landlords available, but often in less desirable areas.

Initial check-in to transition the client from Resource Coordination to Re-entry Navigation, outline Turn 90’s service levels, and establish immediate goals following his recent release to a federal halfway house.

### Program Overview Discussed

Justin outlined Turn 90’s three levels of service:

* **Resource Coordination:** Basic information on available community resources (completed).
* **Re-entry Navigation:** Guided support for goal-setting, resource acquisition, and overcoming specific barriers (Current Phase).
* **First Shift:** An 8-week paid daily program (Mon–Fri, 9 AM–3 PM) focusing on emotional regulation, decision-making, and trade/safety certifications. Participants earn up to $450/week based on punctuality and performance. *Note: The Columbia location currently has a 5–6 week waitlist.*

# Facilitation Evaluation Report

**Location:** Columbia (COL pm 260914)
**Facilitator:** Staff Facilitator
**Evaluator:** QA Director / Lead Facilitator Supervisor

---

### Executive Summary
The observed session demonstrated strong alignment with Turn90 evidence-based CBT facilitation standards. The facilitator effectively maintained a collaborative, non-confrontational tone and demonstrated a solid grasp of core communication skills (OARS, Same-Team Mindset, and Modeling Neutrality).

---

### Detailed Rubric Breakdown

#### 1. Modeling Neutrality & De-escalation (Rating: 4.5 / 5.0)
* **Observation:** When participants shared experiences involving past antisocial or risky behavior, the facilitator stayed grounded and calm, avoiding disapproval or preachiness.
* **Turn90 Standard:** Responding without judgment; focusing on the skill rather than evaluating participant choices.

#### 2. Lesson Plan Adherence & Core Concepts (Rating: 4.0 / 5.0)
* **Observation:** Followed the structured lesson flow (Homework Review -> Buy-In -> Modeling -> Role-Play Prep -> Main Activity -> Close). Minor drift occurred during the Buy-In discussion, which ran slightly long.
* **Turn90 Standard:** Protecting the Main Activity as the core behavioral driver of change.

#### 3. Reflective Listening & OARS Skills (Rating: 4.5 / 5.0)
* **Observation:** Strong use of complex reflections to paraphrase participant meaning and highlight long-term consequences without triggering defensiveness.
* **Turn90 Standard:** Eliciting participant-generated relevance rather than giving unsolicited advice.

#### 4. Avoiding Confrontation & Over-Direction (Rating: 5.0 / 5.0)
* **Observation:** Excellent handling of participant pushback using 'Roll with Resistance' and 'Same-Team' language ("You and me vs. this behavior").

#### 5. Time Management & Class Flow (Rating: 4.0 / 5.0)
* **Observation:** Kept homework review under 18 minutes. Role-play prep was concise, though final debrief was slightly condensed due to initial buy-in expansion.

---

### Actionable Coaching Recommendations
1. **Anchor Definitions On the Board:** Ensure board definitions are written out beforehand to keep group interpretations locked to the curriculum.
2. **Pacing Milestones:** Aim for role plays to begin by Minute 55 to maximize behavioral practice time.
3. **Praise Variety:** Continue to vary verbal and nonverbal reinforcement to celebrate effort over talent.
class_facilitation_evaluations.coaching_feedback: Tighten time management during the initial Buy-In section to protect a full 35–40 minutes for the Main Activity / Role Plays.; Ensure all key definitions are anchored on the whiteboard prior to class or read verbatim from the participant workbook to avoid group interpretation of core concepts.; Increase the use of varied nonverbal expressions of approval (e.g., thumbs up, nodding, leaning in) to reinforce active engagement without interrupting student speech.

## Overview
Thank you for your hard work on this session. Overall, you brought excellent enthusiasm to the room and demonstrated a strong understanding of Turn90's core CBT concepts. Because this was an audio-only review, your physical presence was evaluated strictly through your vocal pacing, tone neutrality, and classroom management. Your voice commanded respect without resorting to authoritarianism, perfectly embodying the **Same-Team Mindset** (Module 1).

## Breakdown of Competencies

### 1. Following the Lesson Plan & Time Management (Score: 3.0 / Acceptable)
While you covered the key concepts of the STAC model (Situation -> Thinking -> Action -> Consequences), your pacing slipped early on. 
* **The Pitfall:** You spent nearly 28 minutes on Homework Review. The Turn90 standard is a strict 15–18 minutes maximum (Module 3.2). 
* **The Impact:** Because you did not utilize a 'Make-Up Zone' (like tightening your modeling or transitions), the Main Activity was rushed. 
* **Coaching Tip:** Remember that CBT is both cognitive *and* behavioral. The behavioral practice (Role Play) is the most important part of the class and must be protected. In the future, use the 'Internal Clock' to cut off repetitive homework reports, ensuring you stick to the 90-minute pacing plan.

### 2. Facilitating Behavioral Practice & Role Play (Score: 3.0 / Acceptable)
Because time was short, the execution of the 1J Upgraded STAC role play suffered.
* **The Pitfall:** You skipped **Setting the Stage** and did not **Begin With the End in Mind**. 
* **Coaching Tip:** Before saying "Action," you must confirm out loud, in front of the group, who the Main Actor is, what the Co-Actor is playing, and how the scene ends (Module 3.3). This prevents the Co-Actor from going rogue and ensures the Main Actor knows exactly what responsible action they are practicing.

### 3. Core Communication & Reflective Listening (Score: 3.5 / Acceptable)
Your questioning was generally strong, but there were moments where you held the facilitation 'rope' too tightly.
* **The Pitfall:** At the 35-minute mark, you began "dating" a participant—engaging in a 4-minute back-and-forth one-on-one conversation while the rest of the group went quiet.
* **Coaching Tip:** Use the **SYNAPSE 'Mirror' method** (Encourage -> Paraphrase meaning -> Reflect the feeling -> Confirm). Once you have validated their point, immediately use an Expand Participation question (e.g., *"What does everyone else think?"*) to bring the group back in and avoid losing momentum.

### 4. Avoiding Confrontation & De-escalation (Score: 5.0 / Very Good)
This was the highlight of your session. When a participant exhibited Attitude Resistance by stating, *"This STAC stuff is pointless, you just react in the real world,"* you handled it beautifully.
* **The Win:** You did not argue or try to convince them (Module 4.4). You used a Level 1 response, acknowledged their reality, and effectively redirected the discussion to the tool and the group (*"For you, these situations happen so fast that stopping doesn't feel realistic. Has anyone else felt that way?"*). This is textbook **Situated Empathy** and kept the classroom completely stable.

## Next Steps
For your next session, your primary goal is **Time Management**. Work backward from the Main Activity to build your time map, set hard milestones, and cut the Homework Review at 18 minutes, no matter what. Keep up the great work with your specific praise and neutral de-escalation!

**Score: Acceptable to Good**

*   **Class Start & Expectations:** The recording begins promptly, and your vocal energy immediately establishes a ready-to-work atmosphere. However, you completely skipped the 2-minute review of classroom rules and expectations. Even with a veteran group, this brief anchoring is a mandatory CBT structure component to maintain the container of the classroom.
*   **Time Management:** Pacing was generally solid. You kept the homework review (1A Practice Using the DMT) to exactly 16 minutes, which perfectly aligns with the 15-18 minute ideal window. You successfully protected the largest block of time for the main role-play activities. 
*   **Lesson Adherence (Role Play Setup):** *[Audio Timestamp 41:15]* There was a notable deviation in fidelity here. During the transition into the main activity for Lesson 1b (Beliefs), instead of guiding the Main Actor to select and approve their own real-life situation, you assigned a hypothetical scenario to them. **Correction:** The curriculum requires the Main Actor to always play themselves in a *relevant, approved situation* from their actual life patterns. Giving them a scenario is a form of over-directing and limits the neuroplasticity and real-world application of the CBT model.

## 2. Group Engagement and Questioning
**Score: Acceptable**

*   **Enthusiasm & Tone:** Excellent. Your vocal modulation shows genuine care for the Spartanburg participants. You sounded deeply invested when explaining the long-term impacts in the DMT 4-Box Analysis, which clearly translated into high group energy.
*   **Avoiding "Dating":** *[Audio Timestamp 24:30]* During the discussion on helpful vs. harmful beliefs, you engaged in an extended back-and-forth with one participant for nearly 4 minutes. While the participant was sharing valuable insights, this turned into "dating" (one-on-one conversation) and excluded the rest of the room. **Coaching point:** After the second follow-up, use the *Pivot to the Group* technique. (e.g., *"That's a powerful realization about fast money. How many of the rest of you have felt that exact same pull?"*)
*   **Buy-in:** You asked excellent, specific buy-in questions. Asking, *"How could using the DMT help protect your freedom in the next 6 months?"* was highly effective and generated great responses. 

## 3. Core Communication Skills
**Score: Good**

*   **Reflective Listening:** You have mastered the *Simple Reflection*. You frequently acknowledged participants by repeating their core points. However, to elevate your facilitation to the next level, you need to introduce *Complex Reflections*. *[Audio Timestamp 32:10]* When a participant said, *"I just don't see how taking a breath stops me from getting disrespected,"* you responded with a question. A complex reflection highlighting ambivalence would have been stronger: *"A part of you knows reacting fast gets you in trouble, but another part feels like pausing makes you look weak."*
*   **Praise and Affirmations:** You use a high volume of positive affirmations, which creates a great emotional environment. However, you over-rely on the phrase *"Good job."* **Coaching point:** Shift to *Specific, Individualized Praise*. Instead of "Good job," try, *"I appreciate the effort you put into breaking down those short-term consequences; you really thought that through."*

## 4. Behavior Management & Neutrality
**Score: Very Good**

*   **Avoiding Confrontation & De-escalation:** *[Audio Timestamp 55:20]* A participant showed clear attitude resistance, audibly sighing and stating, *"This 4-box stuff is a waste of time in the real world."* You handled this masterfully. You did not argue, you did not take it personally, and you maintained your neutrality. You rolled with the resistance beautifully, stating, *"For you, stopping to fill out a grid in a heated moment doesn't feel realistic."* You then effectively redirected to the group. This was a textbook demonstration of the Turn90 same-team mindset. 
*   **Audio-Specific Presence:** Because this is an audio-only evaluation, I listened closely to your verbal cues for physical presence. Your voice was dynamic, moving from different areas of the room (audio panning indicated you were walking the floor during the independent worksheet time). You used verbal check-ins effectively to ensure participants were tracking with the material.

## Summary & Next Steps

You are a naturally gifted facilitator with a deep well of empathy and a fantastic vocal presence that commands the room warmly. You excel at de-escalation and making the participants feel heard. 

**For your next session, please focus on:**
1.  **Do not skip the 2-minute rule review** at the start of class. 
2.  **Approve, don't assign:** Ensure participants generate their *own* real-life situations for role-plays. 
3.  **Practice Complex Reflections:** Challenge yourself to use at least three complex reflections (adding meaning, highlighting conflict) in your next class instead of defaulting to simple reflections or immediate follow-up questions.

# Turn90 Quality Assurance Facilitation Report
**Location:** Columbia
**Date:** September 21, 2026
**Evaluator:** Lead Facilitator Supervisor and QA Director
**Lesson Evaluated:** Module 1: 1d - Thinking Leads to Action (STAC)
**Format:** Audio Review

## Executive Summary
Thank you for your hard work with the Columbia cohort today. Listening to the audio of your session, it is immediately clear that you bring a tremendous amount of heart, enthusiasm, and belief in the Turn90 process to your classroom. Your tone is incredibly supportive, and you do a fantastic job making the guys feel welcome. You have a firm grasp on the STAC (Situation -> Thinking -> Action -> Consequences) model and explained the "Behavior Chain" clearly. 

However, we need to tighten up your time management—specifically during Homework Review—and refine your response to resistance so you don't lose your footing when participants push back. Below is a detailed breakdown of your facilitation based on the official Turn90 CBT Facilitator Scoring Guide.

---

## 🌟 Areas of Strength

**1. Enthusiasm and Tone (Score: 5 - Very Good)**
You bring a highly infectious energy to the room. As outlined in the *Running High-Quality Groups* module, engagement is the engine of CBT, and the facilitator sets the temperature. Your vocal tone was bright, encouraging, and you used excellent positive affirmations ("I hear you," "That's exactly right, man") to validate participation. 

**2. Understanding Core Concepts (Score: 5 - Very Good)**
When introducing the STAC model, you didn't just read from the script; you owned the material. You successfully used the "Go Backward to Go Forward" technique (Core Communication Skills 2.1) by reminding them of the Decision Making Tool (DMT) from earlier in the week and linking it to today's lesson on how thoughts drive actions. 

**3. Specific and Individualized Praise (Score: 4 - Good)**
You made several great emotional deposits today. I specifically heard you praise a participant by saying, *"You really stepped it up today with your STAC breakdown. I can see you put a lot of effort into thinking about the consequences."* This aligns perfectly with praising *effort over talent* and linking praise to specific behaviors (Module 2.4).

---

## 📈 Opportunities for Growth

**1. Time Management & Pacing: The Homework Trap (Score: 3 - Acceptable)**
*Observation:* Your homework review took 26 minutes. 
*The Standard:* According to *Lesson 3.2: Following the Lesson Plan and Managing Class Flow*, Homework Review should take **15–18 minutes, with an absolute maximum of 20 minutes**. 
*The Impact:* Because you lingered in the homework review, you had to rush the Role Play Prep and the Main Activity. The Main Activity is the most important, behavioral part of a CBT class and must be protected above all else. 
*Coaching Fix:* Homework review is a series of mini one-on-one sessions, not a time to re-teach the lesson. Do a quick visual check for 100% completion. Report, quick scan, one affirmation, and move on. If they got it wrong but tried, give them the point, offer a brief redirect, and keep the line moving. 

**3. Role Play Setup: Begin With the End in Mind (Score: 3.5 - Acceptable/Good)**
*Observation:* You got the Main Actor and Co-Actor to the front of the room, assigned roles, and said "Action." But you missed a critical staging step.
*The Standard:* According to *Lesson 3.3: Facilitating Behavioral Practice*, you must **"Begin With the End in Mind."**
*Coaching Fix:* Before saying "Action," you must confirm out loud with the Main Actor exactly what they will say or do to end the scene. Ask directly: *"What are you going to say or do to end this step?"* This prevents the role play from drifting into the "wilderness" and ensures both you and the actors know exactly when you will call "Cut."

---

## 🎯 Action Plan for Next Week

1. **Set a Hard Timer for Homework:** Set a silent timer for 18 minutes. When it goes off, wrap up the final participant and confidently transition into the Buy-in section. Protect your Main Activity time.
2. **Lock in the Ending:** Write "HOW DOES IT END?" at the top of your facilitator guide for the Main Activity. Do not call "Action" until the Main Actor tells you their final line. 

You have immense natural talent as a facilitator and the guys clearly respect you. By tightening up these mechanical boundaries—especially protecting the clock and keeping behavioral roleplay at the center—your classes will go from good to elite. 

Keep up the great work!

Overall Feedback:

**Session Context:** Columbia Afternoon (PM) • October 22, 2026  
**Facilitator:** Jenn Jeanquart • **Cohort:** Small group (2 participants)  
**Curriculum Focus:** Module 8: Support Network (Social Skills: Setting Boundaries)

**Class Arc & Time-Stamped Chronological Observations:**
- **[05:07 - 06:35] Opening & Environment:** Trainees arrived on time and were seated at their desks with workbooks and pens ready ("Woo! Tic-toc, tic-toc", "Today is Thursday"). The room was quiet and orderly.
- **[06:36 - 13:05] Non-Curriculum Digression:** Facilitator spent approximately 6.5 minutes discussing an alleged global internet outage, international hacking threats, stock markets, and her husband's financial bets on materials for bombs and weapons (*"Banking on the fact that we're going to at some point like be in war... morally that's not a good feeling, but he's done really well on the stock"*). While this created informal rapport, it diverted roughly 15% of the total class time away from CBT instruction and introduced themes of violence that contradict prosocial modeling.
- **[13:06 - 15:06] Pivot to Lesson & Buy-In:** Facilitator executed an effective self-aware pivot back to the curriculum (*"That's not my lane. That's his lane. This is my lane... practicing setting boundaries"*). Checked in on morning concepts and asked purposeful buy-in questions: *"What are the four main strategies?"* and *"What problems could it cause if we don't set boundaries well?"*
- **[15:07 - 16:00] Cognitive Skill Steps:** Taught the 3 core thinking steps for the Social Skill of Setting Boundaries: 1) Decide if you want to set a new boundary, 2) Think about what your new boundary will be, and 3) Put the new boundary in place.
- **[15:32] Preparation Hiccup:** Facilitator paused to hunt for the curriculum page in the manual (*"Let's hunt for it. I went ahead to the next lesson, I think. Maybe page 28, 29? Yes, page 29"*).
- **[16:01 - 19:20] Facilitator Role-Modeling (Geoffrey Vignette):** Modeled the thinking steps using Geoffrey's situation (cousin asking for car repair money after release). Demonstrated internal dialogue and saying "no" while setting an expectation.
- **[19:21 - 20:22] Personal Application:** Shared practical guidance regarding personal boundaries with money and lending only what you are willing to lose.
- **[20:23 - 26:29] Participant Worksheet Preparation:** Directed participants to prepare their own realistic scenarios (*"I want you guys to think of a situation where it will be important for you in your life to set a boundary with somebody"*). Supported participants as they completed their thinking steps.
- **[26:30 - 30:00] Roleplay 1 (Automotive Tools):** Participant roleplayed setting a boundary with a nephew who repeatedly borrows tools and failed to return a wrench.
  - At **[27:54]**, facilitator executed a textbook **"Timeout"** intervention: *"Oh, hold on. Timeout. First Before you respond to him, yep. Now use your thinking steps before you set the boundary with him."*
  - Coached participant to state Step 1 (why: need tools) and Step 2 (boundary: nephew can come use tools at the shop, but tools cannot leave).
  - Reinforced boundary firmness at **[29:56]**: *"Right. You turned the 'I can do some, not all' into a no. Like if that's not good enough, then yeah, now this boundary has to be a little bit more firm."*
- **[30:57 - 32:42] Roleplay 2 (Family Addiction / Enabling):** Second participant tackled a vulnerable, high-risk situation involving a family member requesting money for drugs. Stated clear prosocial boundary: *"I know she wants the money for drugs, and I don't want to be an enabler... so I can't give her the money. She needs to start thinking about her sobriety."* Facilitator validated and closed the exercise.
- **[32:43 - 37:16] Early Conclusion & Downtime:** Roleplays concluded early at [32:42] (*"It is mad early. Do the homework on page 31..."*). Left 25+ minutes of unstructured class time that drifted into conversations regarding downtown parking tickets and DMV scheduling rather than conducting a planned CBT extension activity or repeating roleplays.

### 📊 Turn90 QA Facilitator Evaluation Report
**Center:** Charleston  
**Facilitator:** TB (Charleston)  
**Session:** Charleston Morning (AM) - 2026-10-22 - Module 8: Reentry Action Planning & Relapse Prevention  
**Module Detected:** Module 8: Reentry Action Planning & Relapse Prevention  
**Recording Coverage:** 977 transcribed lines spanning 00:02–92:50

### 🕒 What Happened in This Session (from the transcript)
- **[08:29]** Facilitator reviews the homework — _"So, your homework was to respond to three scenarios using the skill of strengthening relationships by being honest."_
- **[18:26]** Facilitator introduces the new lesson — _"we got setting boundaries, 8E. So, in our last few lessons, we talked about making changes in our relationships."_
- **[19:21]** Class watches a video on setting boundaries — _"Hi everybody and welcome back to class today. You are working your way through the upgrading our support network module."_
- **[39:16]** Facilitator sets up a group activity — _"So on page 23, we're going to look at some real-life situations where a person named Jeff needs to set a boundary."_
- **[66:55]** Facilitator introduces the concept of reframing — _"Reframing is changing the way you think about a situation so it helps you instead of holding you back."_
- **[76:56]** Facilitator assigns the next activity — _"So, I'm going to give y'all 5 to 10 minutes. Uh, let's look at how many scenarios it is."_
- **[83:29]** Participants share their responses to the scenarios — _"A friend from your past keeps inviting you to hang out in places where you know there will be drinking, drugs, and risky other, other risky situations."_

| Category | Score |
|---|---|
| Modeling Neutrality | 4.5 |
| Lesson Plan Adherence | 4.5 |
| Reflective Listening | 4.0 |

| Time Management | 4.5 |

| Group Engagement | 4.5 |

### 🌟 Observed Strengths
- **[24:30]** _"You raise a dog as a puppy your whole life, it get loose and bite somebody, and now you got a choice. You got to What do they call it? What is it? Euthanize?"_ — The facilitator uses a vivid, relatable analogy to challenge the group's thinking and explain why setting boundaries can feel harder than cutting someone off completely.
- **[26:36]** _"They set boundaries to strengthen a relationship. That was that's what you was talking about. But no, I like that. - **[39:16]** _"So on page 23, we're going to look at some real-life situations where a person named Jeff needs to set a boundary. You'll work in teams to figure out what boundary issue what the boundary issue is and come up with ideas on how to set the boundary."_ — The facilitator provides clear, structured instructions for the main activity, ensuring participants know exactly what is expected of them before breaking into groups.

### 🎯 Timestamped Coaching Rewrites (What You Said vs. What to Ask Next Time)
| Moment | What Happened | Try Asking This Next Time |

| **[36:24]** | "I mean, for real, though, bro. This serious business, bro. I've seen people get in a whole lot of shootouts. How does keeping that reality in mind help you stick to your own boundaries today?" / "That's a heavy example of how avoiding a tough conversation can lead to violence. | **[35:13]** | "Another response to this is it could cause a relapse. ### 📊 Turn90 QA Facilitator Evaluation Report
**Center:** Charleston  
**Facilitator:** TB (Charleston)  
**Session:** Charleston Afternoon (PM) - 2026-10-22 - Module 5: Problem Solving  
**Module Detected:** Module 5: Problem Solving  
**Recording Coverage:** 397 transcribed lines spanning 04:08–66:28

### 🕒 What Happened in This Session (from the transcript)
- **[24:02]** Facilitator builds rapport — _"So how's your weekend, Joe?"_
- **[28:18]** Facilitator transitions to lesson — _"We're going to continue working on our thinking traps, and then we're going to start getting into some problem solving."_
- **[40:59]** Facilitator guides workbook reading — _"What does it say at the top of page 32?"_
- **[43:00]** Facilitator walks through scenario — _"So let's walk Marcus through the steps. Step one: stop and think. What does Marcus need to do right here in that moment?"_
- **[48:15]** Facilitator sets up roleplay — _"I want you to be yourself. We're going to put you in a situation where somebody bumps into you hard on the street and talks crazy to you."_
- **[48:55]** Facilitator debriefs roleplay — _"And freeze! Timeout. How did that feel?"_

### 📈 Rubric Scores (0–5)
| Category | Score |
|---|---|
| Modeling Neutrality | 4.8 |
| Lesson Plan Adherence | 4.5 |
| Reflective Listening | 3.8 |
| Avoiding Confrontation / Over-directing | 4.8 |
| Time Management | 4.5 |
| Enthusiasm & Energy | 4.6 |
| Group Engagement | 4.5 |

### 🌟 Observed Strengths
- **[48:15]** _"I want you to be yourself. We're going to put you in a situation where somebody bumps into you hard on the street and talks crazy to you. Your job is to use the skill: stop and think, ask what could happen, and decide if it's worth it, and then respond in a way that keeps you out of trouble. You ready?"_ — The facilitator excellently sets up the roleplay by defining the scenario, assigning clear roles, and explicitly stating the skills the participant needs to practice before calling action.
- **[49:29]** _"Exactly. You didn't lose anything that actually matters. You kept your dignity, you kept your peace, and most importantly, you're not sitting in county jail waiting on a bond hearing."_ — The facilitator provides highly effective, specific praise during the debrief, connecting the participant's prosocial choice directly to long-term positive outcomes and freedom.

### 🎯 Timestamped Coaching Rewrites (What You Said vs. What to Ask Next Time)
| Moment | What Happened | Try Asking This Next Time |
|---|---|---|
| **[42:44]** | "Not often. Usually I was just chasing whatever was in front of me." — While the facilitator provides a simple reflection, this is a missed opportunity to use a complex reflection and an open-ended question to explore the participant's underlying motivations for chasing instant gratification. Facilitator said: "Right. The quick reward.". | "It sounds like the immediate payoff felt so urgent that the future didn't even cross your mind. What was it about that quick reward that made it so hard to ignore?" / "You were living completely in the moment. Looking back, how did chasing that instant gratification usually end up working out for you?" |
| **[47:09]** | "Because emotions take over. Your pride get in the way." — The facilitator makes a direct, slightly lecturing statement about pride. To avoid overdirecting and increase buy-in, the facilitator could ask a guided question that leads the participant to articulate this consequence themselves. Facilitator said: "Your pride. That pride will put you in a cell faster than almost anything else.". | "Pride can definitely be a strong trigger. How have you seen pride lead to negative consequences in your own life?" / "When pride takes over, what happens to your ability to stop and think about the long-term consequences?" |

---

# Re-entry Navigation Case Plan: Chance Simmons

## Executive Summary & Clinical Assessment
Participant Chance Simmons is a 40-year-old male under SCDC Reentry Parole Supervision returning to Charleston after serving nearly 20 continuous years of incarceration from age 17. His score-based risk level is **HIGH (23/43)**, heavily weighted by static criminal history and dynamic deficits in **Education/Employment (7/9)**, **Leisure/Recreation (2/2)**, and **Companions (3/4)**. 

Crucially, Chance presents with exceptional protective strengths: **0/4 in Procriminal Attitude** (demonstrates genuine remorse, full accountability, and proactive seeking of psychological counseling) and **0/4 in Family/Marital** (resides in a highly supportive, stable parental home on Johns Island). He has no active acute housing or substance crises.

## Facilitation & CBT Coaching Strategy
- **Modeling Neutrality & Relational Tone:** Adopt an appreciative, encouraging, peer-level coaching tone. Chance is highly sensitive to authority and eager to please; avoid confrontational tactics or power struggles.
- **Targeting Dynamic Criminogenic Needs:**
  1. *Education/Employment:* Transition GED foundation into practical workplace habits, digital literacy, and first-ever community job placement.
  2. *Leisure/Recreation:* Restructure idle TV time into structured daily routines, trade training, and family-oriented prosocial activities.
  3. *Companions:* Insulate against negative neighborhood peer networks by reinforcing family protective factors and workplace social integration.
- **Impatience Management:** When minor impatience surfaces around job search pacing, validate his eagerness to earn while using CBT thought-mapping to highlight incremental progress.

## 90-Day Action Roadmap
1. **Weeks 1–2 (Stabilization & Licensing):** Connect with Father to Father Project for beginner's permit advancement to full driver's license; set up CARTA transit schedules from Johns Island.
2. **Weeks 3–6 (Digital Literacy & Job Preparation):** Conduct 1-on-1 digital application practice; submit tailored applications to local Fair-Chance trade and logistics partners.
3. **Weeks 7–12 (Placement & Maintenance):** Secure entry-level employment; monitor initial supervisor interactions; establish ongoing relapse prevention check-ins.

Subjective (Client's Report)
Current Status & Mood: Client reported feeling "at ease" overall but noted struggling significantly over the past couple of days.
Trauma & Distress: Client experiences recurring, vivid dreams and intrusive thoughts involving the victim of his past offense (occurring ~3 times per week). He expressed deep remorse and guilt, stating he cannot take back his actions and struggles with how others perceive him.
Safety Concerns & Anxiety: Client expressed anxiety regarding potential retaliation from the victim’s family and fears encountering confrontation in public, leading him to keep his head down when walking outside. He noted feeling fearful of getting into future altercations or returning to prison.
Sleep & Coping: Intrusive thoughts and distress interfere with client’s sleep, causing him to wake up early (2:00–3:00 AM) and use music as a distraction.
Relational & Life Goals: Client expressed a strong desire to stay on a positive path, remain out of trouble, and build a meaningful relationship with his 18-year-old daughter. He highlighted his decision to stay away from old associates and locations in Charleston to avoid negative influences.
Peer Support: Client mentioned encouraging his roommate to stay compliant with his medications and using positive coping mechanisms (e.g., walking away from conflicts).
Objective (Worker Observations & Actions Taken)
Client was engaged, reflective, and open about his emotional struggles and past history.
Worker validated client’s feelings of remorse and acknowledged the trauma he is experiencing while reinforcing his progress since release.
Worker guided client through identifying strategies to break negative thought patterns and maintain stability.
Referrals & Outreach:
Worker provided client with the phone number for Eau Claire Behavioral Health to schedule outpatient counseling. Client called the office during the session and left a voicemail requesting an intake callback.
Worker provided client with the emergency crisis line for Columbia Area Mental Health for after-hours or immediate support.
Assessment
Client is demonstrating strong motivation toward successful community reintegration and exhibits key protective factors (family connection with daughter, desire for change, relocation away from high-risk environments).
Client is experiencing symptoms consistent with post-traumatic stress and unaddressed grief/guilt related to his past offense, which manifest as sleep disturbance, emotional distress, and intrusive imagery.
Client shows strong receptivity to professional support and is actively practicing emotional regulation/de-escalation techniques.
Plan & Next Steps
Mental Health Follow-Up: Client to monitor phone for a callback from Eau Claire Behavioral Health to finalize an intake appointment.
Crisis Support: Client encouraged to utilize the Columbia Area Mental Health emergency line if experiencing acute distress or sleep-disrupting intrusive thoughts.
Medical / Program Assistance: Client to return at 12:30 PM to connect with program staff (Kat) via iPad to set up a WellPath referral for prescription medication assistance.
Next Appointment: Follow up with Case Specialist during scheduled check-in to review counseling intake status and progress.

reentry_client_sessions.notes_text:
Client Presentation & Overview Client presented with positive affect, expressively sharing that for the first time in his life—following a 19-year incarceration—he feels like a "real person" and is experiencing genuine happiness. Client expressed deep gratitude for Turn90 staff (Amy, Kat, Justin, and Case Manager), acknowledging the pivotal role the program has played in shifting his mindset and keeping him out of the penal system.

Key Session Discussion Points

Family Reconnection & Support System: Client reported significant progress in rebuilding family relationships. He is actively communicating with his daughters, grandchildren, little brother, and sisters. Client noted he accepted his family's invitation to an upcoming cookout after his daughter encouraged him to attend, seeing it as an opportunity to be present for his kids and grandkids together.
Probation Compliance: Client reported clear communication with his Probation Officer (PO), who approved his travel for the family event. Supervision schedule is currently set for check-ins every two months. Client understands the condition to pay off $1,300 in restitution to qualify for potential early termination of probation.
Employment & Training Goals:
Client expressed high motivation toward obtaining his forklift certification (scheduled to review equipment hands-on next session/tomorrow).
Long-term vocational goals include working in warehouse operations or returning to restaurant work, ideally balancing two jobs to maintain a busy, structured schedule that keeps him out of the streets.
Expressed a desire to learn modern digital financial tools (e.g., Cash App) to manage rent and household expenses independently.
CBT Skills & Risk Management:
Triggers & Behavioral Shift: Client identified his primary trigger as falling back into "old ways" (reacting before thinking, street mentality, and defensiveness developed as prison survival mechanisms).
Turn90 Core Skill Applied: Client highlighted "Stop and Think Before You React" as the most beneficial tool he has learned. He recognized that while his "defense attitude" stems from 57 years of habits and prison self-preservation, he is actively working to let the "new Lawrence" handle situations.
Conflict Resolution & Accountability: Discussed interpersonal dynamics with his roommate. Client identified how verbal escalation or taking the bait during arguments poses a risk to his freedom. Case Manager reinforced accountability regarding his tendency to speak his mind even when wrong, and Client acknowledged the importance of staying calm, de-escalating, and keeping his long-term freedom as the top priority.
Legal Risk Awareness: Client reiterated his firm commitment never to return to prison, emphasizing that carrying a firearm or engaging in street activity would risk a lifetime federal/state sentence and destroy all the progress made with his family.
Next Steps / Plan

Complete upcoming forklift training/certification session.
Assist client with digital literacy skills (setting up/learning electronic payment methods for rent).
Continue weekly 1-on-1 sessions focusing on cognitive-behavioral restructuring, emotional regulation during conflict, and progress toward financial independence.

reentry_client_sessions.notes_text:
## Conversation Summary

This conversation is a case management and mentoring check-in between a Program Manager/Advisor and a client/participant. The dialogue covers personal relationship dynamics, program/class engagement strategies, employment plans, driver's license restoration, substance use and drug testing concerns, credit building, and mental health support.



### Key Discussion Points & Action Items

#### 1. Program Engagement & Classroom Participation

* **Issue:** Client expressed difficulty staying awake during class lectures due to repetitive content and monotonous speaking tones.
* **Discussion:** Client noted he tends to step back from over-participating because he has already completed similar coursework/training and does not want to dominate discussions or disengage peers.
* **Strategies Discussed:** Staying active through physical movement (standing up, shifting around, or doing brief physical exertion like burpees/jumping jacks) and utilizing energy/caffeine options to maintain focus.

#### 2. Relationship & Social Media Concerns

* **Issue:** Client experienced dynamic/relationship friction after posting on the "Threads" app about changing his single status. His partner received a notification via Facebook and expressed feeling hurt and upset.
* **Advisor Guidance:** Discussed navigating communication, acknowledging partner feelings without compromising honest dialogue, and managing online presence.

#### 3. Driver’s License Restoration & Fines

* **Status:** Client has gathered information regarding outstanding fines across Kershaw County and South Carolina.
* **Financial Breakdown:**
* Kershaw County Fine: **$415** (online payment available).
* Total Cap / Expected Cost: **$500+** (including SC DMV reinstatement fees).
* Staff Assistance/Match: Program offers a match up to **$250**. Client plans to contribute **$250** of his own funds.


#### 4. Employment & Vocational Goals

* **Program Status:** Client is currently in an 8-week program ($450/week stipend).
* **Work History & Barriers:** Client has previous work experience (warehouse/cargo, early morning shifts) but struggled with commute barriers and self-sabotage/job retention.
* **Future Options:**
* Union opportunities (post-8-week program completion).
* Security licensing/jobs (event/bar security).
* Content creation (food review TikTok/social media channels once transportation/funds are stable).



#### 5. Credit Building & Financial Literacy

* **Current Credit Score:** ~736 (Client); Partner's score dropped to 600s due to medical bills.
* **Goal:** Rebuild/maintain credit to acquire a reliable vehicle without needing a cash down payment.
* **Topics Covered:**
* Secured credit cards (putting down a deposit, building history, getting deposit refunded upon conversion).
* Pitfalls of high-interest credit lines, buy-now-pay-later services (Klarna), and automatic recurring app subscriptions.
* Avoiding "hard pulls" that drop credit scores unnecessarily.



#### 6. Mental Health & Support Services

* **Discussion:** Client expressed interest in therapy/counseling to manage personal trauma, self-reflection, and avoiding self-sabotage when alone.
* **Resources:**
* Medicaid application submitted (waiting on callback/paperwork).
* Discussed past participation in mentorship/trauma programs (e.g., VIP/Violence Intervention Programs).

Eligible for First Shift after completion of Charleston Center substance abuse program. 

Creating a structured reentry plan for Brian involves addressing several key areas to ensure a successful transition back into society. Here's a step-by-step plan based on the information provided:

### Step 1: Stabilize Living Situation
- **Current Status**: Brian is renting a room from a friend in West Ashley.
- **Action Items**:
  - Ensure the current living arrangement is stable and secure.
  - Explore options for more permanent housing if necessary, possibly with the help of local housing assistance programs.

### Step 2: Address Legal and Probation Requirements
- **Current Status**: Brian is under the Youthful Offender Act (YOA) and on probation.
- **Action Items**:
  - Maintain regular communication with the probation officer.
  - Ensure compliance with all probation requirements, including not contacting the baby's mother directly.
  - Attend all required meetings and check-ins with legal authorities.

### Step 3: Substance Abuse Treatment
- **Current Status**: Brian is attending Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) for substance abuse at the Charleston Center.
- **Action Items**:
  - Continue attending IOP sessions regularly.
  - Engage actively in therapy and support groups to address alcohol-related issues.
  - Explore additional support resources, such as Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) meetings.

### Step 4: Employment and Skills Development
- **Current Status**: Brian has experience in landscaping and some HVAC work.
- **Action Items**:
  - Get on the waitlist for the First Shift program for structured employment training.
  - Work with Daisy, the navigator, to update and refine the resume.
  - Explore job opportunities in landscaping or HVAC that are accessible via public transportation.
  - Consider additional certifications or training that could enhance employability, such as completing the OSHA 10 certification.

### Step 5: Transportation
- **Current Status**: Brian relies on public transportation and occasionally uses Uber.
- **Action Items**:
  - Develop a reliable transportation plan for commuting to work and appointments.
  - Investigate local programs that might assist with transportation costs or provide transportation vouchers.

### Step 6: Rebuild Family Relationships
- **Current Status**: Brian is not in contact with the baby's mother but maintains a relationship with his own mother.
- **Action Items**:
  - Work with a counselor or mediator to explore safe ways to communicate with the baby's mother, respecting legal boundaries.
  - Strengthen the relationship with his mother and seek her support in the reentry process.

### Step 7: Financial Management
- **Current Status**: Brian has some fines related to his driver's license.
- **Action Items**:
  - Work with reentry programs to address and potentially reduce fines.
  - Develop a budget plan to manage expenses and save for future needs, including potential fines and fees.

### Step 8: Education and Personal Development
- **Current Status**: Brian does not have a high school diploma or GED.
- **Action Items**:
  - Enroll in a GED program to improve educational qualifications.
  - Explore personal development workshops or courses that focus on life skills and decision-making.

### Step 9: Health and Well-being
- **Current Status**: No current medical or mental health issues reported.
- **Action Items**:
  - Schedule regular health check-ups to maintain physical health.
  - Continue mental health support through IOP and explore additional counseling if needed.

### Step 10: Regular Check-ins and Support
- **Action Items**:
  - Schedule regular check-ins with Daisy or another reentry navigator to monitor progress and adjust the plan as needed.
  - Utilize community resources and support networks to stay motivated and connected.

By following this structured plan, Brian can work towards a stable and successful reentry into society, addressing key areas of his life that need support and development.

reentry_client_sessions.session_title: Coaching / case management session – structured or in-depth meeting (Terrence Brown)
reentry_client_sessions.notes_text:
### **Summary of Conversation**

The dialogue is a supportive, candid check-in between a participant (Chance) and a mentor/case manager. Chance reflects on his recent progress, personal growth, and challenges after serving 22 years in prison. He discusses maintaining a positive relationship with his mother, managing workplace dynamics and conflict while staying out of personal drama, navigating a recent car accident without reverting to past negative habits, and planning for future career growth (such as moving into forklift driving or HVAC). The session ends with logistics for an upcoming event, a brief phone call with Chance's mother regarding food supplies, and a discussion on mental focus, patience, and astrology.


**Session Type:** Individual Check-in / Mentorship Session

#### **1. Personal Growth & Family Support**

* **Mother’s Support:** Chance expressed deep gratitude for his mother's role as a stabilizing force in his life. He noted that they recently had an open, emotional conversation that helped clear the air.
* **Goal Setting:** Chance stated his primary goal is to purchase a house for his mother so she no longer has to work two jobs at 62 years old.
* **Family Boundaries:** Chance discussed a recent fallout with his cousin. He views this distance as a "graceful way to back away" from toxic dynamics and heavy drinking, allowing him to stay stationary and focused on his priorities.

#### **2. Recent Traffic Incident & Stress Management**

* **Incident Details:** Chance described a recent car accident where a vehicle pulled around another stopped car and hit his vehicle.
* **Coping & Growth:** Despite minor physical injuries and financial stress (paying out-of-pocket for medical checks and ambulance costs), Chance maintained emotional regulation. He highlighted his progress in choosing not to take prescribed narcotics (e.g., oxycodone) due to recognizing his personal risk for addiction, opting instead for non-addictive muscle relaxers.
* **Licensing Status:** Chance is currently working on resolving a paperwork delay regarding his driver's license exam and expects an updated test date next month.

#### **3. Employment & Workplace Dynamics**

* **Current Role & Work Ethic:** Chance reported doing extra work at his current job site (e.g., handling check-ins and station setups) to build a strong reference and demonstrate a solid work ethic.
* **Interpersonal Navigations:** He described managing workplace conflicts among staff and female managers by remaining neutral, avoiding workplace politics, and focusing solely on his work.
* **Future Employment Goals:** Chance views his current job as practice and intends to transition into higher-paying roles ($20+/hour), specifically targeting forklift operation and eventual growth into trades like HVAC.

#### **4. Mentorship & Program Engagement**

* **Program Perception:** Chance expressed high respect for the mentor/program, noting that the honest, direct feedback ("un-cut") resonates with him and encourages growth.
* **Community Influence:** Chance discussed using his credibility and history to encourage younger individuals to take rehabilitation programs seriously and avoid self-destructive behavior.

reentry_client_sessions.session_title: Coaching / case management session – structured or in-depth meeting (Terrence Brown)
reentry_client_sessions.notes_text:
**Overview**
This conversation is a case-management or counseling session following up on an individual ("Chance") who served 22 years in prison and is working on reintegration, behavioral control, and self-development. The dialogue covers his progress, internal struggles with anger/violence, strategies for self-regulation, personal goals, and interpersonal challenges.

---

**Key Themes & Discussion Points**

* **Reintegration & Adaptation:**
* Chance spent 22 years in prison (after 2 years in juvenile detention) and had been home for only 5 months prior.
* He acknowledges having "arrested development" and is focusing on retraining his mind to adapt to society rather than relying on prison survival instincts.


* **Managing Violence, Energy, and Temper:**
* **Internal Battle:** He describes struggling with a "dark side" and aggressive impulses. He references a scene from *The Hurricane* where the character faces three versions of himself (scared, evil, middle) while in the hole.
* **Trigger Event:** Recounted an incident on his 40th birthday where a woman snatched his necklace. His immediate impulse was extreme violence (popping/shooting her), but he managed to step back to avoid returning to prison and harming his family's reputation.
* **Energy Regulation:** He notes that his high energy/excitement can come off as aggressive or paranoid to others. To manage this, he practices keeping his hands down, slowing down, and mentally role-playing scenarios in his car before encountering stressful situations.


* **Self-Medication vs. Mindset:**
* He drinks socially on weekends to relax, but denies using alcohol as an angry coping mechanism.
* They discuss the risk of using alcohol/substances to self-medicate anger and touch on whether proper medication or alternative physical outlets (like returning to a workout plan) would help regulate his mood without losing his autonomy.


* **Goals & Self-Development:**
* **T-90 Goal:** Preparedness for employment and securing a job (working toward an entry-level restaurant/kitchen job to start small and avoid getting overwhelmed).
* **Core Goals:** Patience, self-development, breaking the habit of constantly dwelling on/talking about prison stories, and building new life experiences.
* **Family Motivation:** Wants to avoid going back to prison or dying, as both outcomes deeply hurt his tight-knit family.


* **Interpersonal Dynamics & Communication:**
* **Classroom / Group Setting:** His facilitator addresses his tendency to be long-winded, which leads to people cutting him off or losing the main point ("word salad"). Chance accepts the feedback, recognizing he needs to state points concisely for maximum impact.
* **Navigating Confrontation:** Shared a recent incident where a former acquaintance tried to intimidate/provoke him. Chance de-escalated the situation by staying calm, addressing the threat directly without violence, and walking away.

reentry_client_sessions.session_title: Coaching / case management session – structured or in-depth meeting (Terrence Brown)

Here is a summary of the session along with structured case notes based on the transcript provided:

---

## **Session Summary**

The client discussed their thinking patterns, emotional triggers, and history with incarceration and substance use. Turning 40 has prompted a shift in perspective—the client emphasized wanting to build a long-term legacy rather than chasing short-term rewards or quick fixes.

Key discussion points included:

* **Thinking & Behavior:** The client recognized a tendency to blame others to avoid taking accountability, often using excuses to cover up feelings of impatience or laziness.
* **Incarceration & Arrested Development:** Arrested at 17 and serving significant time, the client reflected on how prison acts like a "time chamber" or "daycare" that stunts personal and emotional growth. The client acknowledged that emotional maturity requires taking active responsibility rather than falling back into old survival mindsets.
* **Goals Moving Forward:** The client wants to focus on building a legacy for their future family, developing patience, practicing active listening, and avoiding impulsive decisions driven by short-term stress or negativity.

---

## **Case Notes**

### **Client Information**

* **Age:** 40
* **Status:** Post-release (released December 31st; approx. 8 months post-incarceration)
* **Session Type:** Individual Case Management / Reentry Counseling

---

### **1. Thinking Patterns & Focus Areas**

* **Primary Cognitive Pattern (B4):** Focusing on short-term rewards/what feels good now rather than long-term impact.
* **Secondary Cognitive Pattern (B2):** Blaming others rather than examining personal responsibility.
* **Triggers Identified:**
* Situations requiring patience or slow processes.
* Feeling blamed, criticized, or stressed when things do not go as planned.



---

### **2. Substance Use Focus**

* **Primary Pattern (F2):** Using substances (historically cocaine, weed, alcohol) to cope with stress or difficult emotions.
* **Triggers Identified:** Anger over being blamed or feeling overwhelmed by external pressures/frustrations.
* **Goal:** Re-engage with healthy outlets (e.g., returning to working out/physical fitness).

---

### **3. Skills Selected for Practice**

* **Skill 23:** Responding to criticism (listening to feedback without deflecting or pointing fingers).
* **Skill 5 / Skill 3:** Deciding to be responsible and apologizing / taking verbal accountability.
* **Social / Self-Management Skills (Skills 7, 12, 17):**
* Identifying emotional triggers that increase the urge to use substances.
* Practicing healthy coping strategies during stressful moments.
* Stopping and thinking before making decisions related to substance use.



---

### **4. Action Plan / Homework**

1. **Identify Personal Role:** Identify personal involvement/responsibility in at least one conflict this week.
2. **Active Listening:** Practice active listening during at least one disagreement.
3. **Verbal Accountability:** Verbally take responsibility in one situation without making excuses.

---

### **5. Counselor Notes & Next Steps**

* Client demonstrates strong self-awareness and a genuine desire for growth, though there is a risk of over-analyzing external circumstances or attempting to control uncontrollable situations.
* Weekly sessions are scheduled for **Tuesdays** to review progress on action items, practice target skills, and support long-term stability and legacy-building goals.

reentry_client_sessions.session_title: Intake Appointment COMPLETED (Justin Evans)
reentry_client_sessions.notes_text:
Summary
Discussing re-entry program enrollment, navigating license revocation, and establishing financial literacy strategies for stabilizing employment outcomes.

Re-entry Program Enrollment
Participation in the re-entry program is currently pending due to a 2-week waiting list. Commuting remains a challenge requiring resolution before active enrollment begins.

License Reinstatement Strategy
Negotiating with the Department of Social Services is necessary to address driver's license revocation. Reducing the required lump sum payment is the priority for regaining driving privileges.

Employment and Financial Support
Guidance will focus on resolving credit issues and identifying local interim employment opportunities. Stability is the primary goal for long-term successful reintegration.


Next steps
[Justin Evans] {Search Local Work}: Investigate employment opportunities near Berkeley County for the participant.
[Justin Evans] {Email James Swick}: Communicate with James Swick at the child support enforcement division regarding potential license reinstatement steps.
[Justin Evans] {Send Action Steps}: Compile and text the participant a summary of necessary tasks and instructions by tomorrow.
[Justin Evans] {Research Financial Resources}: Find and provide information regarding banking and credit restoration for the participant.
[Morris Hayward] {Contact Department of Social Services}: Call the license revocation unit to discuss current status and reinstatement requirements.
[Morris Hayward] {Request Reemployment}: Contact Mavis Academy to inquire about potential job openings.
[Morris Hayward] {Request Loan}: Ask family members for financial assistance to cover the license reinstatement fees.


Details
Participant Background and Re-entry Goals: Morris Heyward met with Justin Evans to seek support after their release from the Alcanon Detention Center on August 15 following incarceration for child support arrears. Morris expressed a strong desire to avoid further incarceration, secure stable employment, and utilize the organization's resources to get back on their feet.
Program Participation and Transportation Challenges: Justin Evans described the organization’s paid re-entry program, which operates Monday through Friday, 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM, and functions on a point-based payment system. Morris resides in Berkeley County, near Cypress Garden Road, and lacks a valid driver's license, creating a significant barrier to commuting for the program. Justin Evans placed Morris on the waiting list for the program, noting that enrollment might take approximately two weeks.
Driver's License Revocation and Child Support Strategy: Morris lost their commercial driver's license due to child support arrears and is seeking to reinstate their regular driving privileges. Justin Evans explained that Morris must contact the license revocation unit of the Department of Social Services (DSS), present their situation, and ask for a reduction of the lump sum payment typically required for reinstatement. Justin Evans provided the DSS child support division phone number (1-800-768-5858) and advised Morris to explain their financial situation to a caseworker to negotiate a manageable payment plan.
Legal and Financial Literacy Guidance: Justin Evans offered to provide guidance through the re-entry navigation process to assist with tasks such as resolving legal barriers and improving financial literacy. Morris specifically requested help with banking and credit issues to recover from the financial strain of incarceration. Justin Evans committed to staying in communication with Morris to help navigate these matters and to send further information via text to outline the steps clearly.
Employment Opportunities: Morris is actively searching for employment and mentioned potential interest in returning to Mavis Academy in Goose Creek, a former employer. Justin Evans encouraged this approach, noting that Morris's lack of a violent or inappropriate background should allow for potential re-employment. Justin Evans also agreed to investigate interim work opportunities closer to Morris's residence in Berkeley County to help them gain stability.
Coordination and Next Steps: Morris planned to call the driver's license revocation unit on the day of the meeting and follow up with Justin Evans the next day to report the results of that call. Justin Evans confirmed that Morris would receive assistance with these resources regardless of their status on the paid program waiting list.
Post-Meeting Debriefing and Casual Conversation: Following the consultation, Morris discussed the meeting details with an unnamed third party, summarizing the two-week waiting list and the specific advice provided regarding the driver's license and child support legal support. This informal concluding dialogue also touched on logistical topics such as P.O. box requirements, daily household needs, and an extended, non-professional conversation regarding sports, specifically concerning LeBron James.

reentry_client_sessions.session_title: Coaching / case management session – structured or in-depth meeting (Diyoung Dantzler)
reentry_client_sessions.notes_text:
Shelah demonstrated increased insight into his personal risk factors and how his decisions can affect his progress\. He was able to identify that being mindful of his surroundings and considering how others may perceive his reactions can help him avoid unnecessary consequences\. He acknowledged that he sometimes gives himself excuses for small mistakes and identified the importance of setting boundaries with himself and making more responsible decisions\. Shelah continues to use his free time constructively by searching for employment opportunities on Indeed and remains focused on obtaining stable employment and transportation\.

**Barriers:**
Shelah arrived late Monday following his previous suspension related to difficulty managing his emotions while speaking on the phone in a public parking area\. Transportation continues to be a barrier despite Shelah recently obtaining his driver’s license\. He acknowledged that he has not consistently followed through with available transportation resources, including Dial\-A\-Ride, and identified forgetfulness as a factor that can interfere with following through\. He also recognized that becoming comfortable or making excuses for small issues could potentially lead to larger consequences, including stagnation or procrastination toward his goals\.

**Goals:**
Shelah’s immediate goal is to obtain a job interview with a company located close enough to reduce transportation difficulties and expenses while he works toward obtaining his own vehicle\. He also identified the need to become more consistent with transportation planning, follow through with available resources, arrive on time, and continue developing emotional self\-control and personal accountability\.

**Intervention:**
Case manager used motivational interviewing and accountability\-based questioning to help Shelah examine the connection between his decisions, consequences, and long\-term goals\. Shelah was asked what he could have done differently regarding the previous phone incident\. He identified that he could have ended the conversation and addressed the matter after work rather than risk his employment by reacting publicly\.

Following his late arrival Monday, Shelah was held accountable and informed that continued lateness could jeopardize his participation\. Discussion focused on the importance of communicating when circumstances may cause him to be late and taking proactive steps to prevent transportation problems\. Shelah identified that he could arrange transportation ahead of time or contact staff for assistance\.

Case manager revisited the previously provided Dial\-A\-Ride resource after Shelah acknowledged that he had not followed through with using it\. Through discussion, Shelah recognized that failing to utilize available resources could lead to discouragement and reinforce the belief that things are not working for him\. He identified forgetfulness as an area that he needs to address\.

Case manager also explored Shelah’s understanding of personal risk factors and accountability\. Shelah stated that learning about his risk factors surprised him because he had not previously recognized how certain habits and behaviors were contributing to problems in his life\. He acknowledged that having knowledge is not enough and that he must apply what he is learning to his daily decisions\.

Shelah was encouraged to view accountability as an opportunity for growth rather than a reason to give up\. He identified that accountability can help him become more responsible and avoid developing tunnel vision\. He also recognized the importance of using his free time constructively and preparing ahead of time for potential transportation issues\.

**Next Steps:**

- Shelah will contact Dial\-A\-Ride before 10:00 a\.m\. to begin utilizing the transportation resource provided\.
- Shelah will plan transportation in advance rather than waiting until the last minute\.
- Shelah will communicate with staff as soon as possible when an unexpected transportation issue occurs\.
- Shelah will continue using Indeed and other employment resources to seek employment\.
- Shelah’s goal for the week is to obtain an interview with a company located close to him to reduce transportation barriers and expenses\.
- Shelah will continue working toward obtaining reliable personal transportation and eventually a vehicle\.
- Shelah will continue practicing emotional regulation, personal accountability, and following through with available support resources\.
- Case management will continue monitoring punctuality, transportation follow\-through, employment progress, and Shelah’s ability to apply knowledge of his personal risk factors to daily decision\-making\.

Strengths

Shelah continues to show increased awareness of the behaviors and thought patterns that support his goals. He identified the importance of balancing discipline and motivation and allowing himself time to respond rather than react to unexpected situations. He recognizes how easily he can be pulled back into old patterns and is working toward developing healthier behaviors.

Shelah has also been making progress in rebuilding his relationship with his daughter. He recognizes the importance of understanding her feelings and being intentional about strengthening their relationship. He identified his current support system as an important influence in helping him remain focused and accountable.

Barriers

Shelah continues to struggle with accepting help from others because he prefers to handle things independently and does not like feeling indebted to anyone. He acknowledged that refusing assistance can sometimes create unnecessary barriers and close doors to opportunities. He is working on recognizing that not everyone has negative intentions when offering support.

He also identified limited time during the day to handle important responsibilities, particularly with businesses and services closing before he is finished with programming. He understands that employment will need to provide a healthy transition that allows him to continue managing these responsibilities.

* Continue developing discipline and consistency in his daily routine.
* Break old behavioral patterns and practice responding instead of reacting.
* Strengthen his relationship with his daughter.
* Complete his OSHA certification and forklift certification.

* Continue working with Vocational Rehabilitation for additional support.
* Explore career options based on his skills, interests, and talents.

Shelah was encouraged to examine his current influences, how he spends his free time, and whether those influences support or interfere with his goals. We also discussed the importance of accepting appropriate support and understanding that receiving help does not necessarily create a debt or obligation.

Case management also reinforced the importance of time management, completing responsibilities before the end of the day, and developing a realistic employment plan that supports his transition. Shelah completed his first meeting with Vocational Rehabilitation and is seeking additional assistance.

Next Steps

Shelah will work toward scheduling or completing his driver’s license appointment, continue his OSHA and forklift certifications, and follow up with Vocational Rehabilitation regarding additional resources. He will also explore potential career fields and identify at least one area of interest to begin researching.

Shelah will continue practicing the difference between reacting and responding, accepting appropriate support, managing setbacks, and maintaining accountability to his goals. He will also continue working on strengthening his relationship with his daughter and using his current support system to remain focused and productive.
